Hourly vs Salary: Which Pays More? $32 an Hour Against a $65,000 Salary, Worked Out

Direct AnswerHourly vs salary: $32 an hour is $66,560 a year, beating a $65,000 salary by $1,560 — until unpaid weeks flip it. Effective rates, overtime, taxes worked out.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 3, 2026•13 min read•Calculation Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: Hourly Wins the Headline, Salary Can Win the YearWhat Hourly and Salary Actually MeanThe Headline Math: $66,560 Against $65,000The Effective Rate: What a Salary Really Pays per HourWhat Overtime Does to the ComparisonThe Flip: How Unpaid Weeks Hand It to SalaryThe Other Flip: When Hours Get CutPricing the Benefits Package in DollarsHourly vs Salary After Taxes (Federal Only)When Each One WinsThe 6-Question Checklist Before You ChooseHow to Use the CalculatorsLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

$32 an hour is $66,560 a year full-time, beating a $65,000 salary by $1,560 gross — but two unpaid weeks flip it to a $1,000 loss, and a 50-hour salary week cuts the salary to $25.00 an hour.

The Short Answer: Hourly Wins the Headline, Salary Can Win the Year

Hourly vs salary is not a personality question; it is an arithmetic question with four variables. Take a concrete pair: $32 an hour against a $65,000 salary. At a standard full-time year of 2,080 hours, the hourly job pays $66,560 gross — $1,560 more than the salary. After federal tax alone, the hourly job still leads by $1,247.46 of take-home pay. That is the headline, and it is where most comparison pages stop.

The rest of this guide is why the headline is not the answer. A salary week that actually runs 50 hours pays only $25.00 an hour. Two unpaid weeks on the hourly side erase the lead entirely and turn it into a $1,000 deficit. A 3% retirement match on the salary side adds $1,950 that the headline never counts. And five overtime hours a week — paid at $48 an hour — push the hourly job to $79,040, a figure no fixed salary in this comparison can touch. Work through all four variables before you choose, and use the checklist at the end to score your own two offers the same way.

What Hourly and Salary Actually Mean

An hourly worker is paid for every hour worked. A salaried worker is paid a fixed annual amount divided into equal paychecks, whatever the hours in a given week. That single difference drives everything else: hourly pay rises and falls with the schedule, salary pay does not.

One trap catches more people than any other: salary does not mean exempt. Exempt status — which removes overtime pay — comes from job duties plus a salary test (currently $684 a week for the main exemptions), not from being paid a salary. A salaried employee who is non-exempt still earns overtime past 40 hours. Conversely, an hourly employee is almost always non-exempt and therefore overtime-eligible. If you are comparing offers, ask for the classification in writing; a “salary” label alone tells you nothing about overtime. Our exempt vs non-exempt guide works through the three tests.

Benefits follow a similar pattern: they are correlated with salary jobs, not guaranteed by them. Many full-time hourly roles carry full health coverage and paid time off, and some salaried roles carry thin benefits. Never assume the package — price it, as the benefits section does below.

The Headline Math: $66,560 Against $65,000

Both offers on the same footing — a full-time year, before tax, before benefits:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Hourly annual gross$32 × 40 hours × 52 weeks$66,560.00
Step 2 — Salary hourly equivalent$65,000 ÷ 2,080 hours$31.25 per hour
Step 3 — Headline gap$66,560 − $65,000$1,560.00 to hourly
Step 4 — Hourly weekly / biweekly / monthly$1,280 / $2,560 / $5,546.67Gross, before tax
Step 5 — Salary weekly / biweekly / monthly$1,250 / $2,500 / $5,416.67Gross, before tax

At 40 hours a week the hourly rate is worth $0.75 an hour more than the salary ($32.00 against $31.25). That is the whole headline advantage — $0.75 × 2,080 hours = $1,560. Everything after this section is about the conditions that shrink, erase, or reverse it. Our hourly-to-annual conversion guide covers the conversion itself in more depth.

The Effective Rate: What a Salary Really Pays per Hour

A salary buys your week, not your hour. The honest comparison divides the salary by the hours you will actually work — and salaried weeks routinely run past 40:

Real weekly hoursAnnual hoursEffective hourly rateWhat it costs you
40 (as advertised)2,080$31.25Nothing — the headline holds
452,340$27.78260 unpaid hours a year
502,600$25.00520 unpaid hours; now $7.00 below the hourly rate
552,860$22.73780 unpaid hours; below the national median wage

At 50 hours a week, the $65,000 salary pays $25.00 an hour — $7.00 an hour less than the $32 hourly offer, or $18,200 less across the 2,600 hours actually worked (2,600 × $7.00). Ask current employees how long the week really runs before you sign; the job description says 40, the calendar decides. This is the single most common way a “better” salary quietly loses.

What Overtime Does to the Comparison

Overtime is where the hourly offer pulls away — if you are non-exempt and the hours actually exist. At time-and-a-half, each overtime hour pays $48 instead of $32. With 5 overtime hours every week, all year:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay40 hours × $32$1,280.00 per week
Step 2 — Overtime rate$32 × 1.5$48.00 per hour
Step 3 — Overtime pay5 hours × $48$240.00 per week
Step 4 — Weekly total$1,280 + $240$1,520.00 per week
Annual total$1,520 × 52$79,040.00

Five steady overtime hours add $12,480 a year, lifting the hourly job $14,040 above the salary — and the effective rate for that 45-hour week is $33.78 an hour ($1,520 ÷ 45), higher than the base rate itself. The honest caveat runs the other way too: overtime that exists on paper but never materializes is worth $0, and overtime that pushes you into exhaustion is not free money. Price only the overtime you can verify — ask how many overtime hours the team averaged over the last quarter. Our overtime calculation guide and overtime calculator run the same math for your own rate.

The Flip: How Unpaid Weeks Hand It to Salary

Paid weeks are part of the hourly offer, not a footnote. At $32 an hour, each unpaid week costs exactly $1,280 of gross pay:

Paid weeksPaid hoursAnnual grossAgainst the $65,000 salary
52 (fully paid year)2,080$66,560.00Hourly ahead by $1,560
50 (2 unpaid weeks)2,000$64,000.00Salary ahead by $1,000
48 (4 unpaid weeks)1,920$61,440.00Salary ahead by $3,560

Notice how small the flip is: the $1,560 headline lead survives only 1.2 unpaid weeks ($1,560 ÷ $1,280). Two unpaid weeks do not just erase it — they reverse it. And the recovery is cheap, which is worth knowing before you negotiate: one overtime hour every other week across the 50 paid weeks is 25 hours × $48 = $1,200, more than closing the $1,000 gap and lifting the year to $65,200. Ask how many weeks are paid before accepting any hourly offer, because the answer moves the result more than the rate itself.

The Other Flip: When Hours Get Cut

Salary pay is immune to a slow week; hourly pay is not. If the hourly schedule drops from 40 hours to 32 hours a week — a common cut in retail, hospitality, and seasonal work — the year becomes $32 × 32 × 52 = $53,248, which is $11,752 below the salary and $13,312 below the fully-paid hourly figure. A cut to 35 hours still costs $8,320 a year ($58,240). The salary, meanwhile, pays $65,000 whether the week is busy or dead.

This is the risk premium salary carries: you trade upside (overtime) for a floor. If your hourly hours have been stable for a year and the employer guarantees a minimum schedule in writing, the risk is small. If hours already swing with the season, budget from the low-hours year, not the headline year — and weigh the salary’s floor accordingly.

Pricing the Benefits Package in Dollars

Comparison pages usually wave at benefits (“salary jobs have better benefits”) without pricing them. Price them. Take a typical salary package against a bare hourly offer:

StepMathValue
Step 1 — Salary baseFixed annual pay$65,000.00
Step 2 — 3% 401(k) match$65,000 × 3%$1,950.00
Step 3 — Salary cash value$65,000 + $1,950$66,950.00
Step 4 — Two paid weeks the hourly job lacks2 × 40 × $32$2,560.00 of paid time
Step 5 — Salary package vs fully-paid hourly$66,950 vs $66,560Salary ahead by $390
Step 6 — Salary package vs 2-unpaid-week hourly$66,950 vs $64,000Salary ahead by $2,950

One modest match alone — 3%, before any health coverage value — erases the hourly headline lead. Add employer health contributions and the gap widens further; subtract them (an hourly role with equal benefits) and the hourly lead stands. The method is the point: list every benefit line, put a dollar figure on each from the offer letter, and add it to the base before you compare. Our pay stub guide shows where 401(k) and premium lines land on a real paycheck, and the FICA guide explains the one deduction that hits both offers identically.

Honesty note: the $2,560 paid-time figure is time value, not extra cash — the salary worker is paid for two weeks they do not work, while the unpaid hourly worker simply is not paid. It belongs in the comparison because time off has real value, but it is not spendable income.

Hourly vs Salary After Taxes (Federal Only)

Tax does not pick a winner between pay types — it only follows the income. For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, here is the federal-only sketch for both offers. State tax, 401(k), and health premiums are excluded, so real paychecks will be lower:

StepHourly: $66,560Salary: $65,000
Step 1 — Standard deduction− $16,100.00− $16,100.00
Step 2 — Taxable income$50,460.00$48,900.00
Step 3 — Federal income tax$5,813.20$5,620.00
Step 4 — FICA (7.65%)$5,091.84$4,972.50
Take-home (federal only)$55,654.96$54,407.50
Monthly / biweekly take-home$4,637.91 / $2,140.58$4,533.96 / $2,092.60
Keep rate / marginal bracket83.6% / 22%83.7% / 12%

The hourly job keeps $1,247.46 more — less than the $1,560 gross gap, because its last $60 of taxable income crosses into the 22% bracket ($50,460 against the $50,400 threshold) while the salary’s $48,900 stays entirely in the 12% bracket. Federal tax on the hourly side is 10% × $12,400 + 12% × $38,000 + 22% × $60 = $5,813.20; on the salary side it is 10% × $12,400 + 12% × $36,500 = $5,620.00. A page that taxes either offer at a single flat rate will get both wrong. The method matches our paycheck tax guide and the after-tax series (see the $29-an-hour guide for the same bracket steps at a lower income).

Honesty note: this sketch assumes all pay counts as wages for both income tax and FICA, with no pre-tax deductions. A 401(k) contribution would lower the income-tax lines but not the FICA lines; cafeteria-plan health premiums would lower both.

When Each One Wins

The whole comparison in one table — including the limitation each win carries:

SituationWinnerMarginLimitation
Straight 40-hour weeks, fully paidHourly+$1,560 grossAssumes no unpaid time and no benefits gap
5 overtime hours a week, all yearHourly+$14,040 grossNeeds non-exempt status and real overtime hours
Two unpaid weeks on the hourly sideSalary+$1,000 grossCloses with 25 overtime hours across the year
Salary week actually runs 50 hoursHourly$7.00 an hourExempt salary only; non-exempt salary still earns overtime
Hours cut to 32 a weekSalary+$11,752 grossAssumes the salary survives the same slowdown
Salary adds a 3% 401(k) matchSalary+$390 cash valueMatch vests on the employer’s schedule, not day one

No row wins on its own. Your offer is one row, not the table — find your row, then check the limitation column before you act on it.

The 6-Question Checklist Before You Choose

Run both offers through these six questions, in order, and write the dollar figure for each. The offer with the higher total after question 5 — adjusted by question 6 — is the better financial deal:

  1. How many weeks are paid? Multiply the hourly rate by paid weeks, not 52. Two unpaid weeks cost $2,560 here.
  2. How many hours will you really work? Divide the salary by real annual hours. A 50-hour salary week is $25.00 an hour, not $31.25.
  3. Are you overtime-eligible, and how many overtime hours are real? Five real overtime hours a week are worth $12,480 a year at this rate; promised hours that never arrive are worth $0.
  4. What is each benefit worth in dollars? Add the match, the paid time, and the employer health contribution from the offer letters — not from memory.
  5. What is the after-tax gap? Same income, same tax. Only the gross gap survives tax, slightly shrunk — $1,560 gross became $1,247.46 here.
  6. What breaks first? Hours cut, overtime dried up, or a 50-hour salary week — which downside can your budget absorb? The offer that survives its worst realistic case is often the right one even when it loses the headline.

Limitations

  1. Federal only: the after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. State and local income taxes are excluded, so actual take-home is lower.
  2. Benefits priced, not guaranteed: the 3% match and two paid weeks are an illustrative package from the comparison, not a market average. Your offer letters decide the real figures.
  3. Overtime is conditional: the $79,040 overtime figure needs non-exempt status, actual overtime hours, and an employer that pays past 40 hours.
  4. Schedule assumptions: figures use the schedule stated in each section; fewer hours, unpaid weeks, or longer salary weeks change every number.
  5. Exempt status is fact-specific: the duties tests and the $684-a-week threshold are summarized here; classification disputes turn on the actual job, not the title.
  6. Not tax or legal advice: the take-home sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. Credits, other income, and filing status change your real return.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about hourly vs salary pay:

Is it better to be paid hourly or salary?

Neither is always better — it depends on hours, overtime, paid weeks, and benefits. On the headline in this guide, $32 an hour ($66,560 a year) beats a $65,000 salary by $1,560. But if the hourly job has two unpaid weeks, it falls to $64,000 and loses by $1,000; if the salary job adds a 3% 401(k) match, its cash value rises to $66,950. Run the six questions in the checklist section before deciding.

Do you get taxed more on salary or hourly pay?

No. Tax depends on how much you earn, not on how your pay is labelled. A $66,560 hourly income and a $66,560 salary would face the same federal income tax and the same FICA. In this guide the hourly job takes home $1,247.46 more only because it earns $1,560 more gross — $55,654.96 against $54,407.50, federal only, single filer 2026.

Is salary always better than hourly?

No, and overtime is the clearest counterexample. Five overtime hours a week at $32 an hour add $12,480 of gross pay a year ($79,040 total), which no fixed salary matches unless the salary itself is higher. Salary wins when the hours are long and unpaid, the benefits are strong, or the hourly schedule is unstable — the effective-rate and benefits sections price each case.

How do you convert a salary to an hourly rate?

Divide the salary by the hours you actually work, not by 2,080 by default. $65,000 ÷ 2,080 hours is $31.25 an hour at a true 40-hour week, but the same salary at 45 hours a week is $27.78, and at 50 hours it is $25.00. Our salary-to-hourly calculator does the division; the effective-rate section shows why the hours you enter matter more than the headline salary.

Can a salaried employee get overtime pay?

Yes, if the employee is non-exempt — salary is a pay method, not an exemption. Exempt salaried employees (the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions, with the $684-a-week salary test) get no overtime pay. Non-exempt salaried employees do earn overtime for hours over 40. Check your classification, not your pay label; our exempt vs non-exempt guide explains the tests.

How do I compare two job offers, one hourly and one salary?

Annualize both on the same basis, then adjust in this order: paid weeks, realistic weekly hours, overtime, benefits priced in dollars, and finally after-tax pay. The checklist section walks through all six steps with the $32-an-hour and $65,000 figures, and the salary comparison calculator runs two offers side by side with commute time and paid time off included.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $32 an hour is $66,560 a year full-time — $1,560 ahead of a $65,000 salary on the headline, $1,247.46 ahead after federal tax alone.
  • A 50-hour salary week pays $25.00 an hour, not $31.25 — divide every salary by the hours you will actually work.
  • Five overtime hours a week add $12,480 a year ($79,040 total) — the hourly offer’s biggest lever, if the hours are real.
  • Two unpaid weeks flip the result: hourly falls to $64,000, $1,000 behind the salary — recoverable with 25 overtime hours across the year.
  • A 3% 401(k) match alone erases the headline lead: salary cash value rises to $66,950, $390 ahead of fully-paid hourly.
  • Salary does not mean exempt: non-exempt salaried workers still earn overtime — check classification, not the pay label.
  • Tax follows income, not pay type: the same $66,560 faces the same tax whether it arrives hourly or salaried.
  • Run the 6-question checklist on your own two offers — paid weeks, real hours, real overtime, priced benefits, after-tax gap, worst case.

Sources & Method

Gross figures use the standard full-time year of 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks); monthly averages divide the annual total by 12 and biweekly figures use 26 paychecks. The after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), with both incomes below the wage base. The exempt-status summary reflects the FLSA duties tests and the $684-a-week salary test for the main exemptions. State income tax, retirement contributions, health premiums, bonuses, and tips are excluded except where a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The headline favours hourly here: $66,560 against $65,000, or $1,247.46 of take-home after federal tax alone.
  2. Real hours, paid weeks, overtime, and priced benefits each move the result by more than the headline gap — check all four.
  3. Salary is a pay method, not an exemption — and tax follows income, not the label on your paycheck.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 3, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
